cells.tense: You are tending something now and it is showing the work, here at the bench.
cells.ask: Name what you've grown to one person who didn't see it happen, and say what it took to get there.
cells.core:
Whatever you've been looking after is coming up now — not someday, this week. You watch it and you adjust, water here, wait there, and the thing responds. That back-and-forth is the whole of what's happening, and it's working. Care that isn't straining, a result you can point at.

So say it out loud. Tell one person what you've grown and what it took, someone who missed the slow part. Saying it isn't for them, it's for you — it closes the job in a way that quiet work doesn't. You've held this steady for a while. Let the sentence land where the harvest already is.
cells.sheetLine: Something you tended is bearing fruit, and you can say so.
cells.verb: Tending something through to a visible harvest
cells.place: Where care for what is growing gets done

cells.tense: You are already past the harvest, bracing for the next thing to fail before it has grown.
cells.ask: Stop at one thing that's already grown and spend two minutes with it. Don't plan the next.
cells.core:
You're living out ahead of the result. What's growing is fine, and you're somewhere past it — checking what's next, planning the upgrade, guarding against the day this stops. The care has turned into watching for trouble. Nothing you tend gets to arrive, because you're already braced for the version that doesn't.

The cure is in the room with you. Stand still with one thing that already worked. The harvest is real; the person who tended it left to guard the door. Come back and be where the finished thing is. That's not resting, that's the only way to see what's actually in front of you.

cells.tense: You walked away from a patch you were tending, and you are still standing at that door.
cells.ask: Pick one thing to grow for its own sake this season and put the first hour on the calendar this week.
cells.core:
Something you were looking after got left behind. Maybe it stopped being wanted, maybe the work stopped, maybe the whole patch got let go — but the bench is there and nobody's at it. You don't call it loss. You call it over and done with. Meanwhile every new thing gets eyed from a distance, like it might ask more than you have.

What's left is care with nowhere to land. Point it at one thing first — the size doesn't matter yet. A single plant, a single project, one hour this week. The first hour is the whole ask; what it becomes after is a later question. Starting is smaller than you're making it right now.

cells.tense: You are growing something and calling it just what happened, as if the garden came up on its own.
cells.ask: Pick one result you credit to luck or timing, and say out loud, once, that you grew it.
cells.core:
You already bring things along. The timing, the patience, the showing up — it's running, and it produces something the people around you can see. On the healthy side of this, the grower says so plainly: planted, kept alive, here it is. The fruit gets kept and the credit gets taken aloud. What happens instead is the same work filed under luck, or circumstances, or the notion that it came up on its own. Same hands, same hours, no claim attached.

So the doing is real and the tallying isn't. Sit with one instance long enough to see the shape of what you did, then say it once, for your own ears. The work doesn't need the credit, but you're the one carrying it, and carrying a thing you're already doing is lighter than saying you aren't.
cells.sheetLine: Something grew under your hands and you're calling it luck.

attempts.check: Unsupported claim: that the 'still standing at a door that's already behind you' past-anchor is a real dynamic in this person's life, not just a template reading. A reader could reasonably say they're not blocked at all, they simply have nothing growing right now worth tending. The ask still works if my read is wrong, since naming one star and defending one hour a week is useful even for someone beginning fresh rather than recovering. The sentence that serves me more than them is 'You can tell which one is yours' in the Balanced cell, which flatters my insight rather than their situation; I've cut it to something they can verify or reject.
